description: The Residential Test Facility at NIST in Gaithersburg, Maryland, first known as the Net-Zero Energy Residential Test Facility, is both a laboratory and a two-storey house with four bedrooms and three bathrooms, used as a testbed for cost-effective residential systems that give healthy and comfortable indoor environments. It was designed to be about 60 percent more energy efficient than homes meeting the 2012 International Energy Conservation Code, and is operated with a simulated family of four. Over its first year it exceeded its net-zero goal, exporting a surplus to the grid, and in the second year a different setup of subsystems quadrupled the surplus. The team continues to study systems and operating strategies for high-performance homes. Coverage: one test house in Maryland, United States. Access: NIST pages with results, publications and contacts; measurement datasets are published separately by NIST. Licence: U.S. government work; free. Caveats: the virtual occupancy removes real occupant behaviour, and the results are for one climate and design. Simulation uses are validation data for residential energy models, heat pump and ventilation control studies and net-zero design benchmarks. Related records: EnergyPlus and ResStock.

name: NIST Net-Zero Energy Residential Test Facility (Residential Test Facility, Gaithersburg)
outcomes: In its first year (July 2013 to June 2014) the all-electric house met all its energy needs from on-site renewables with a surplus of 484 kWh, enough to drive an electric car about 1,400 miles, against an estimated $4,400 electricity bill for a comparable Maryland home; in the second year, with changed heating and ventilation operation and milder weather, the surplus rose to 2,139 kWh.
provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Engineering Laboratory
resources_used: Simulated occupancy of a virtual family of four
